messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Elias had finished his final route on a Friday evening when his body first betrayed him. Eighteen hours on the wheel had left his shoulders knotted, his vision blurred, and a bone-deep weariness that felt less like fatigue and more like physical surrender. Walking from the depot to his parked sedan, he took a narrow service road behind the maintenance barn. He remembered the sudden scrape of rubber on damp asphalt, then the immediate, shocking weight of a man pressing him into the chain-link fence. Hands pinned his wrists. A voice gave sharp, demanding orders. The terror was absolute, paralyzing him in a way he had never known, and when it was over, he lay against the cold metal mesh for a long time, listening to the distant rumble of traffic, certain he would never feel safe again. The exhaustion he had felt that night quietly became a silent alarm. Whenever his body grew heavy after a long shift, his breath would catch, his neck muscles tightening as if bracing for a blow he could no longer outrun. He stopped taking service roads. He began checking his car locks three times. On his route, the sight of a passenger stepping onto the bus sent a cold wire through his chest. He told himself it was just caution, but in the quiet spaces between stops, he was certain that driving with others meant vulnerability. Certain that the space between his driver’s seat and the boarding door was a boundary that could be breached without warning. When he finally allowed himself to drive his personal car again, having even a single passenger beside him made his palms sweat and his grip white-knuckle the steering wheel. At night, sleep offered no refuge. His mind would flip open like a projector, playing the service road in relentless loops. He did not just remember the event; he relived the exact terror he had felt when his body had been pinned, the same frantic pounding in his chest, the same suffocating dread. Alongside the terror came a deep, scalding shame that settled over him as the sequence replayed. He felt ashamed of his body for not fighting harder, for going limp, for being placed in that position. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted, that the world had quietly turned hostile behind his back. His faith in any higher power had evaporated alongside his sense of safety; he no longer prayed, only sat in the dark wondering why the silence had answered him with violence. Over the following months, avoidance took root. He began requesting evening routes, where the few remaining passengers were strangers he would never see again. He avoided long-haul shifts that demanded extra hours, knowing his diminishing stamina would only sharpen his fear of exhaustion. He stopped driving his personal car on crowded evenings. He withdrew from weekend dinners, from neighborhood gatherings, from the casual conversations that once filled his kitchen. His wife, Clara, noticed how he flinched when the refrigerator door shut, or how he sat rigidly still whenever a car backfired outside their window. He had not told her about the shame that clung to his skin, or how he now saw his own reflection in mirrors as something fractured. His work performance suffered not from incompetence, but from a careful, exhausting calculation of every sound on the road: the sudden hiss of a pneumatic door, the thud of a dropped bag, the specific cadence of footsteps that matched the alley that night. Now, at fifty-three, the weight of years has settled into his joints. He came to this office after Clara gently placed a referral card on the dashboard of his bus, her eyes wide with a fear that mirrored his own. He is here because the loops will not stop, because the exhaustion feels less like fatigue and more like a warning signal, and because he no longer knows how to distinguish between a present moment and a past that refuses to fade. He hopes, despite everything, that the terror might finally quiet. He fears, more than anything, that he has already ruined the safety of his own life, and that the man he was before the fence has disappeared forever.
